extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for beginners on writing short jokes and stand-up material, covering point-of-view, premise generation, joke structure, editing, and live testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define your POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Your comic POV is the lens through which you see ALL material. It's not a topic; it's an attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Things designed to help us actually make us miserable."; "Adults are children with money."; "Modern intimacy is just well-dressed loneliness." If you can't articulate your POV, every joke will feel like it could belong to someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate premises (write opinions daily)
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 minutes a day, write down opinions you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each opinion, ask: who would disagree, and why? The disagreement is a comedic engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure: Intro / Setup / Punch / Tag
rubrics_metrics.description: State the premise plainly (this is your INTRO line). Add evidence/example (this becomes the SETUP). Subvert the example (this is the PUNCH). Hit the same target from a different angle (this is the TAG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this sequence to build a joke that orients the audience, establishes expectations, then subverts them and extends laughs with a tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut, cut, cut (edit ruthlessly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the joke. Time it. Cut every word that doesn't earn a laugh or load the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-time after edits. Aim to cut 30% on first edit. Rule of thumb: a 14-word joke is almost always better than a 21-word version of the same joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test in public
rubrics_metrics.description: Try it on three different audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke that works once is a coincidence. A joke that works three times is a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Does this joke fit your POV (would only YOU write it)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the joke uniquely reflects your comic point-of-view such that it would only come from you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it could belong to someone else, refine the premise or voice until it clearly fits your POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Is the premise an opinion, not an observation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the core premise is an expressed opinion rather than a mere neutral observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinionated premises create stakes and invite disagreement, which drives comedy (see Generate Premises guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Does the punch reverse the example?
rubrics_metrics.description: The punch should subvert or reverse the expectation set by the example in the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns with the 'subvert the example' instruction in Joke Structure; effective reversal creates the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Have you cut at least 30% from the first draft?
rubrics_metrics.description: On first edit, remove roughly 30% of words that don't serve the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a measurable editing target; timing and re-testing after cuts are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Has it landed in three different rooms?
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm the joke has worked for three distinct audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as live validation that the joke is robust beyond a single successful trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's Rubric: Did you record yourself and cringe productively?
rubrics_metrics.description: Record performances and review them critically to learn from delivery, timing, and mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-recording helps identify issues that aren't apparent while performing and fuels productive edits.
